messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: ordering of limits in scale_*_continuous
parts:
Hi everyone,

previously ggplot seemed to be smart and sort the vector in the limits
argument before using it. I.e.:

library("ggplot2")

d=data.frame(a=runif(10),b=runif(10))

ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=-b)) +
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,-2))
# used to be equivalent to:
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=-b)) +
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-2,0))


Was it a voluntary change to remove that behaviour? Can it be re-
enabled, at least for the sake of backward compatibility? I am
currently going over some one year old code and I am hitting all kinds
of problems due to changes in ggplot. I am conscious that one year is
a long time in the life of ggplot2 but overall, it is still a pretty
short time.

Thanks in advance.

JiHO

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Re: ordering of limits in scale_*_continuous
parts: On 2009-May-17  , at 16:50 , Mike Lawrence wrote:

> It's debatable whether the previous behaviour is "better" than the
> current behaviour. I like that the current behaviour lets you flip the
> direction of the axis by flipping the limits.

I see the utility of this indeed. I was really asking because of
backward compatibility. ggplot might be young enough that backward
compatibility is not be the prime concern. It's just that I have gone
back through one of my major projects and I spent nearly 3 days just
fixing things that got broken because of changes in ggplot (and
reshape). My hope is that, now that the book is out, the syntax will
stay fixed a little bit. Reliability is not a virtue that people might
seek at first (so this does not impact ggplot's success currently),
but I think it is ultimately what makes people stick to anything (be
that a computer program or a pen or a bank or...). When things get
broken/changed a lot, even for the best of reasons, people get tired
of adapting.

JiHO

ggplot is in version 0.8.3, that is, Hadley hasn't yet declared it to
be "version 1".

It seems to me perfectly appropriate that Hadley continue to make
incompatible changes until then.  And even then, presumably whatever
is documented in the book is pretty much frozen, but there is no
commitment that *undocumented* behavior be frozen -- taking advantage
of that is at the user's risk....

I would certainly hope that our feedback as beta users will influence
the future design of the system....

            -s

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Re: ordering of limits in scale_*_continuous
parts:
library("ggplot2")

set.seed(1)
d=data.frame(a=runif(10),b=runif(10))

ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,1))
# OK
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(1,0))
# 10 rows removed

ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=-b)) +
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-1,0))
# OK
ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=-b)) +
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,-1))
# 10 rows removed


So indeed it looks like a bug. I initially thought it was only
occuring with a negative mapping of the data, as -b above. Basically
that it would cut out the data that was not on the plot based on the
original values rather than the transfromed(i.e. negative) ones. But
it seems more general than that.

JiHO

> # 10 rows removed

> scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-1,0))
> # OK
> ggplot(d) + geom_point(aes(x=a,y=-b)) +
> scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,-1))
> # 10 rows removed
>

> So indeed it looks like a bug. I initially thought it was only
> occuring with a negative mapping of the data, as -b above. Basically
> that it would cut out the data that was not on the plot based on the
> original values rather than the transfromed(i.e. negative) ones. But
> it seems more general than that.

When you use xlim or ylim, if the order is flipped, then it uses
scale_x_reverse. If you use scale_continuous with limits, no data
will be plotted because it's checking that the data is bigger than the
first value and smaller than the second.

The next version will automatically sort the limits and eliminate this problem.

Regards,

Hadley
